sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text: Kaiserslautern, in the Palatinate, says that demand for parking in its inner city exceeds supply, and regulates it with two paid zones. The fee ordinance in force from 1 May 2023 splits paid on-street parking into a core zone, with 1.00 euro per 30 minutes and a three-hour maximum stay, and an outer zone, with 1.00 euro an hour or a day ticket of 5.00 euros, charged Monday to Saturday from 8:00 to 19:00 except public holidays [0]. An earlier ordinance of 2019 charged 0.50 euro per 25 minutes in the core zone and 3.00 euros a day in the outer zone, so the core rate rose from about 1.20 to 2.00 euros an hour, though the changes may have come in steps [1]. The city says its aims are efficient use of spaces for customers, visitors and residents, higher turnover through the three-hour limit, and a stronger incentive to use bus, rail, bicycle and walking [3]. A resident permit costs 100 euros for six months, 200 euros for a year or 400 euros for two years since 1 February 2024, and a paywalled newspaper teaser says the annual fee in the inner city rose from 30 to 200 euros, with about 8,000 permits in circulation [2]. Since 15 July 2026 the city has 14 new paid 30-minute short-stay spaces in Richard-Wagner-Straße and Eisenbahnstraße, where resident permits no longer apply during charging hours, and the new machines are the city's first card-only ones [4]. Electric cars with an E plate may park free at on-street charging posts while charging, for at most three hours [17]. The Stellplatzsatzung of March 2022 sets how many spaces new buildings must provide, and the developer can pay an in-lieu amount of 5,700 to 12,700 euros per space [5].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The city's mobility work centres on the new K in Lautern shopping centre. A city page says its arrival set off a new inner-city traffic concept, with the works at Fruchthallstraße and Fackelbrunnen started in September 2022 and essentially finished in autumn 2023, and the Burgstraße section expected from 2024, with its current status not stated [16]. The mobility plan Klima+ 2030, adopted on 5 February 2018, rests on a survey of November 2016 that counted about 2,600 spaces in 12 city-centre car parks and about 2,590 on the street, and found car-park occupancy partly below 20 percent and rarely above 70 percent, while street parking was often overloaded; this is nearly ten years old [13]. A survey of 2023 found that half of all trips are made by car, 3.5 points fewer than in 2018, and that about two thirds of cars are parked on private spaces [14]. For home matches at the Fritz-Walter-Stadion, SWK runs free shuttles from the park-and-ride sites, since there is no public parking in the Betzenberg area, though the page contains older text and its currency is uncertain [15].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The city runs a parking guidance system with 34 dynamic signs in four areas, Centrum Nord (990 connected spaces), West (1,020), Ost (530) and Hauptbahnhof (360), with live counts on its website [6]. Contipark runs Parkhaus City Löwenstraße with 400 spaces and Parkhaus Lutrinastraße with 220, both with limited opening hours and no Sunday opening for City, at 1.50 euros for each of the first two half-hours and a daily maximum of 16.00 euros [7]. The Hauptbahnhof P2 garage has 359 spaces, is open round the clock and costs 2.00 euros an hour or 12.00 euros a day [8]. Park Service Hüfner runs the Altstadtparkhaus Rittersberg, with 372 spaces, and Parkhaus Pfaff Areal, with 361 [10], and Q-Park the Pfalztheater (296) and Stiftsplatz (180) garages [11]. APCOA lists the K in Lautern garage with 490 spaces, closed on Sundays, while the city's page still refers to Q-Park for its fees, so the current operator is unclear [12].

Our data cover ten car parks, but only about 13 days and roughly one reading a day for each, so the figures are rough, and the feed's capacities are lower than the operators' (for example 230 against 400 for City and 175 against 372 for Altstadt), so the percentages are relative to the feed. On that basis the Altstadt car park averaged 91% on weekdays and 86% at weekends, and reached full in single readings, City 83% and 71%, Lutrinastraße 81% and 44%, Sparkasse 75% and 64%, and the Meuthstraße lots about 70% on weekdays and 52% at weekends, while Pfalztheater averaged 70% and 61%. The Hauptbahnhof garage fell from 56% on weekdays to 16% at weekends, which fits commuters, and Stiftsplatz stayed near 55% every day. One further feed, PH Central, shows the same value in every reading, so we do not treat it as a measurement.
